sections.h2: Ways to sell fast in Harrison
sections.html:
Harrison owners can list with an agent, sell privately, or accept an as-is cash purchase. Only the cash route skips staging, showings and renovation deadlines. Median home values here run above $1 million, so a rushed sale can cost real money. Hold any offer up against what comparable Harrison houses have sold for.

Harrison is a combined town and village in Westchester County, about 27 miles from Grand Central. That setup gives sellers one building department for the whole municipality, a Receiver of Taxes who collects several times a year, and a county clerk who records the deed.

  • Agent listing: works when the house is market-ready and you have time to spare.
  • Private sale: avoids the commission, but negotiation and paperwork fall on you.
  • Cash purchase: for estates, unfinished projects, tenant-occupied homes or a fixed deadline.

Harrison had 32,273 residents in 2025, up from 28,218 in the 2020 count, living in 9,222 households of about 2.88 people. Owners occupy 60.5% of homes. The median owner-occupied value is $1,010,700, median rent is $2,616, household income is $164,250 and the commute averages 29.2 minutes. Because the median sits just over $1 million, many Harrison sales reach the level where the state's 1% mansion tax applies. The buyer pays it.

The town is shaped roughly like a figure eight. Downtown Harrison lies in the south, with Purchase and West Harrison to the north. Downtown breaks into Brentwood Plaza, Sunny Ridge, Sterling Ridge/The Trails and the Village part, with Halstead Avenue as its main street. West Harrison, around Lake Street and Silver Lake Park, has few road entrances. Purchase holds Manhattanville University and SUNY Purchase, and Westchester County Airport lies almost entirely within it. Harrison station on Metro-North's New Haven Line is the commuter link, and I-95, I-287, I-684, the Hutchinson River Parkway, NY 120, 120A and 127 cover the roads. The Bee-Line runs buses.

Much of the older housing dates from the 1920s through the 1950s. Sunny Ridge was laid out on a former farm after 1929, and most of its colonial revival and Tudor houses went up from the mid-1940s on. Owners of period homes should keep records of past renovations, since buyers of older houses ask for them.

The Harrison Central School District runs Harrison High School and Louis M. Klein Middle School, both downtown, plus four elementary schools. Purchase School covers Purchase and the north of West Harrison, Preston covers the Silver Lake area, Parsons covers south downtown, and Harrison Avenue School covers the rest of downtown. Elementary zones follow neighborhoods, so a Sunny Ridge address and a Purchase address feed different schools. Name the zone when you describe the house.

The Assessor's Office keeps a record card on each of roughly 7,000 parcels and values them using current sales and cost, then the tax rate is applied to produce each bill. The Receiver of Taxes collects town, village, school, county and state tax from a single office in the Municipal Building.

Harrison assessment and tax calendar
DateWhat happens
May 1Taxable status date; exemptions due
June 1Tentative roll filed; grievance period opens
Third Tuesday in JuneGrievance period ends
September 15Final roll filed
February and JuneTown and village tax due
January and SeptemberSchool tax due
AprilCounty and state tax due

Bills are mailed before the first of the month and must be paid by the month's last day. Mailing is a courtesy, and a lost bill doesn't excuse a late payment. Report a change of ownership to the tax office in writing.

Harrison requires a building permit for new buildings, additions, alterations and accessory structures, and the Building Inspector issues the Certificate of Occupancy. A buyer's attorney will look for both on any house with visible improvements.

Most residential construction needs Architectural Board of Review approval. Permits also cover sheds, decks, pools, interior alterations, fences, driveways, tree removal, plumbing and electrical work. After new construction, additions, accessory structures, fences, walls or altered driveways, the department may ask for a final as-built survey. The Assessor learns of finished work from the permit and inspects with the Building Inspector before adjusting the assessment, so an unpermitted addition can show up as a code problem and a higher bill at once.

  • Collect permits and Certificates of Occupancy for each improvement.
  • Find the latest survey; the department wants 36 by 48 inches at standard size.
  • Counter hours run 9am to 5pm, and applications go in person or by mail, not electronically.

Harrison deeds are recorded by the Westchester County Clerk's Land Records Division. The fee schedule lists a $45 statutory fee, $5 per written page, $5 for the TP-584 form on residential property and $125 for the RP-5217 transfer report. The clerk steers filers to its PREP portal to work out the fees due.

New York's transfer tax is $2 for each $500 of price, rounded up, and the seller normally pays it. The 1% mansion tax at $1 million or more falls on the buyer.

sections.h2: Why records matter on an older house
sections.html: A good share of Harrison's houses were built decades ago and have been added onto since. Each project leaves a trail: a permit, an inspection and, for larger work, a final survey and a Certificate of Occupancy. When a buyer's attorney sees an addition without that trail, the sale slows while someone sorts it out. The Building Inspector's office is the place to ask what is on file for your address, and it is much easier to ask before you list than during a contract.

sections.h2: Closing steps for a Harrison seller
sections.html:
After you accept an offer, your attorney sends a contract and the buyer's side orders title work. Missing permits or a missing Certificate of Occupancy will surface there, so gather those first. At closing you sign the deed and transfer forms, your lender's payoff comes out of the proceeds, and the deed goes to the county clerk. Cash buyers can often close sooner because there is no mortgage underwriting, but ask for the closing date, proof of funds and a split of costs in writing before you commit.

Tax proration follows the calendar above. A closing in spring or summer means school and town installments may be partly paid, so ask the Receiver of Taxes for a printout of what is open.

faqs.q: Does Harrison have separate town and village taxes?
faqs.a: Harrison is one combined town and village, and the Receiver of Taxes collects both, with payments due in February and June. School tax is billed separately for January and September, and county and state tax in April.

faqs.q: When can a Harrison owner contest an assessment?
faqs.a: The grievance period runs from June 1, when the tentative roll is filed, to the third Tuesday in June. The Assessor sets May 1 as the date exemptions are due, and the final roll is filed September 15.

faqs.q: Is a permit needed for a deck or shed in Harrison?
faqs.a: Yes. Sheds, decks, pools and interior alterations all need permits, and most residential construction also needs Architectural Board of Review approval. The Building Inspector issues the Certificate of Occupancy.

faqs.q: What does the buyer pay on a million-dollar Harrison sale?
faqs.a: A 1% mansion tax applies when a residence sells for $1 million or more, and the buyer pays it. The seller covers New York's base transfer tax of $2 per $500, paid at recording.

faqs.q: Where is a Harrison deed filed?
faqs.a: With the Westchester County Clerk's Land Records Division. A recording needs the deed, form TP-584, form RP-5217 and the filing fees, which the clerk's PREP portal can calculate.
